events.text: Jekyll wakes in bed and finds he has become Edward Hyde.
events.quote: I had gone to bed Henry Jekyll, I had awakened Edward Hyde

events.text: Dressed as Hyde, Jekyll passes through the house and Bradshaw stares and draws back.
events.quote: Bradshaw stared and drew back at seeing Mr. Hyde at such an hour and in such a strange array

events.text: Ten minutes later Dr. Jekyll returns to his own shape and feigns breakfast.
events.quote: Dr. Jekyll had returned to his own shape and was sitting down, with a darkened brow, to make a feint of breakfasting

events.text: Jekyll reflects seriously on the issues and possibilities of his double existence.
events.quote: I began to reflect more seriously than ever before on the issues and possibilities of my double existence

events.text: Jekyll fears the balance of his nature may be permanently overthrown.
events.quote: the balance of my nature might be permanently overthrown

events.text: Jekyll notes the drug's power has not always been equally displayed and once failed.
events.quote: The power of the drug had not been always equally displayed

events.text: Jekyll realizes he is slowly losing hold of his original and better self.
events.quote: I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self, and becoming slowly incorporated with my second and worse

events.text: Jekyll feels he must choose between his two natures.
events.quote: Between these two, I now felt I had to choose

events.text: Jekyll chooses the better part but lacks strength to keep to it.
events.quote: I chose the better part and was found wanting in the strength to keep to it

events.text: Jekyll prefers the elderly doctor and bids farewell to Hyde's pleasures.
events.quote: I preferred the elderly and discontented doctor

events.text: Jekyll keeps the Soho house and Hyde's clothes as an unconscious reservation.
events.quote: I neither gave up the house in Soho, nor destroyed the clothes of Edward Hyde

events.text: After two months of severity, Jekyll again swallows the transforming draught.
events.quote: in an hour of moral weakness, I once again compounded and swallowed the transforming draught

events.text: Jekyll is punished by Hyde's moral insensibility and readiness to evil.
events.quote: it was by these that I was punished

events.text: Jekyll listens with impatience to the civilities of his unhappy victim.
events.quote: I listened to the civilities of my unhappy victim

events.text: Jekyll mauls the unresisting body with delight from every blow.
events.quote: I mauled the unresisting body, tasting delight from every blow

events.text: Jekyll flees the scene, destroys his papers in Soho, and walks the lamplit streets.
events.quote: I ran to the house in Soho, and (to make assurance doubly sure) destroyed my papers

events.text: Hyde drinks the draught and pledges the dead man.
events.quote: Hyde had a song upon his lips as he compounded the draught, and as he drank it, pledged the dead man

events.text: Henry Jekyll falls on his knees with tears of gratitude and remorse.
events.quote: Henry Jekyll, with streaming tears of gratitude and remorse, had fallen upon his knees

events.text: Jekyll resolves that Hyde is thenceforth impossible and locks the door.

facts.quote: My devil had been long caged, he came out roaring

rels.desc: Jekyll and Hyde share one body and memory but unequal faculties.
rels.quote: My two natures had memory in common, but all other faculties were most unequally shared between them

relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls Hyde trampling a girl, then paying her family £100 with a genuine cheque. Utterson studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful and has never heard of Hyde. Keeping watch, Utterson accosts Hyde, who admits Jekyll is out, gives a Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. Poole confirms Hyde has a key and all servants must obey him. Jekyll pales when Utterson mentions Hyde, refuses more, but says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses. He asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when gone.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death. The mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Guest finds the murderer’s letter identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After the murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, then shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. But this danger was easily eliminated from the future, by opening an account at another bank in the name of Edward Hyde himself; and when, by sloping my own hand backward, I had supplied my double with a signature, I thought I sat beyond the reach of fate.
[P8] Some two months before the murder of Sir Danvers, I had been out for one of my adventures, had returned at a late hour, and woke the next day in bed with somewhat odd sensations. It was in vain I looked about me; in vain I saw the decent furniture and tall proportions of my room in the square; in vain that I recognised the pattern of the bed curtains and the design of the mahogany frame; something still kept insisting that I was not where I was, that I had not wakened where I seemed to be, but in the little room in Soho where I was accustomed to sleep in the body of Edward Hyde. I smiled to myself, and in my psychological way, began lazily to inquire into the elements of this illusion, occasionally, even as I did so, dropping back into a comfortable morning doze. I was still so engaged when, in one of my more wakeful moments, my eyes fell upon my hand. Now the hand of Henry Jekyll (as you have often remarked) was professional in shape and size; it was large, firm, white and comely. But the hand which I now saw, clearly enough, in the yellow light of a mid-London morning, lying half shut on the bedclothes, was lean, corded, knuckly, of a dusky pallor and thickly shaded with a swart growth of hair. It was the hand of Edward Hyde.

He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment.
